A highly clever and comedic script combines with an all-star cast to create a spot-on satire.
Lindsay-Abaire's fresh and funny comedy uses the pettiness, blind spots and outright biases of the diverse characters who are involved to comment with sharp insight on The Way We Live Now.
Here, the playwright takes a simple conceit and mines it for hilarious social satire featuring a gallery of memorable characters played by a top-flight cast.
Top-notch comedy and covetable home decor—all in a tidy 100-minute package.

The Neighborhood Association is meeting this week in the gorgeous, newly renovated home of neighborhood newcomer Kyra (Anika Noni Rose), a Black doctor (race is not mentioned here casually; stay tuned), who is eager to get involved in her new surroundings and just as eager to forget what happened at her old surroundings.

Lindsay-Abaire's masterwork is surely the 2011 play Good People, a devastating dissection of class division in South Boston memorably led on Broadway by Frances McDormand (also at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, where Balusters now makes its home).

It’s never easy to reconcile preaching with satire, though, and unfortunately, “Balusters” seems more concerned about reinforcing lessons that will sit comfortably with a Broadway audience than taking a candid look at the issues and conflicts it addresses.
With so many outrageous lines done to a fare thee well from this sensational acting ensemble, The Ballusters provides more gut-busting laughter than any show this season.

Under Kenny Leon’s superb direction, each performer offers up a precise characterization and peerless line deliveries, all of which make this extremely enjoyable show even funnier and more profound than it is on the page.

The Victorian house at the epicenter of David Lindsay-Abaire's new Broadway play, The Balusters, is a stunner. Scenic designer Derek McLane's stunning front parlor, replete with coffered ceilings and wide archways that lead to the dining room and beyond, is a dream out of Architectural Digest.

The Balusters is the latest in a series of contemporary stage comedies that are less interested in traditional drawing rooms than in drawing blood — skewering the foibles and hypocrisies of progressive lefties who also happen to be theater’s most reliable ticket buyers. In the opening line I said the show made me sick, and it didn't get any nicer from there. Rabbit Hole was about well-to-do Westchester parents grieving the senseless, accidental death of their young boy. There's talk about pocket universes where grief is eternal and the concept helps the sorrow-frozen protagonists achieve closure or peace.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).

Headout and SeatPlan both flag rows E-J as the best price-to-sightline ratio: meaningfully cheaper than the A-D premium band while staying close in a 634-seat room. Slight orchestra rake keeps sightlines clean. Mezzanine overhang (per SeatPlan) begins at row G but the intimate room means no sound-deadening issue in this band.

sg.vl: Under the overhang but still engaged
sg.ra: SeatPlan confirms the Mezzanine overhangs from row G back, so K-Q sit fully under. The room is small enough (Headout: 'one of Broadway's more intimate spaces') that rear orchestra remains engaged. Rows P and Q are accessibility-friendly (no aisle stairs per folliesbroadway). Legroom tightens beyond row O per SeatPlan.

Headout and SeatPlan both name AA-BB center as premier seats with 'clean, direct look at the stage' and elevation that improves the view. aviewfrommyseat user on Mezzanine L row A aisle reported 'lots of legroom' with only a thin safety bar as minor issue. Excellent rake across the mezzanine.

SeatPlan and Headout both emphasize that the mezzanine has 'excellent rake' keeping all rows elevated with clean sightlines; Headout says 'no truly bad seat in the house'. Small 224-seat mezzanine means even row G stays close. Row F offers transfer seats and row E has wheelchair spaces (Headout accessibility).
